Investment memo · HTO-GR · Hellenic Telecom (OTE): the investment case, what drives it, and what would move the shares

Hellenic Telecom (OTE) is a highly predictable cash distributor: its return is a high floor of dividends and per-share earnings growth, plus whatever multiple Greece pays

Investment memo for Richard, 8 November 2026. Share price EUR 18.78 (6 November 2026); market value about EUR 7.3bn; two-year-forward P/E 10.8x on the model's basis. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model (update 1), unchanged. Definitions of EBITDA, EPS and free cash flow, and the reasons for leaving the forecast inputs unchanged, are in the end notes.

#0 Summary: the key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line for Richard

Own OTE for an unusually skewed return: about +19% over 18 months from dividends and per-share earnings at an unchanged multiple, about +29% at my fair multiple, and roughly zero even at a crash multiple.

OTE is not a growth or recovery story. OTE is a cash machine with top-decile foundations, whose share price depends on the multiple Greece pays, not on European telecoms.

Two dates decide the next 18 months: the December 2026 tariff announcement (the size of the early-2027 price step) and the 25 February 2027 results day (the FY2027 guide and the distribution).

OTE's foundations are among the best in European telecoms. OTE is Greece's incumbent operator and is 54.6% owned by Deutsche Telekom. OTE takes 65% of Greek telecom revenue, 73% of the industry's EBITDA and 93% of its operating free cash flow. OTE earns a 42% EBITDAaL margin and a 29% return on equity, carries net debt of only 0.5x EBITDA and is the only A-rated corporate in Greece. When the Public Power Corporation (PPC) entered fibre broadband at half OTE's price, PPC failed to win even 1% of OTE's broadband base.

The case is a highly predictable cash distributor, not a growth story and not a recovery story. OTE pays out almost all of its underlying free cash flow of about EUR 575m (the payout policy is 70% to 100%), two-thirds as dividend and one-third as buyback. The declared FY2026 dividend of EUR 1.02 (consensus expects EUR 0.96) is a 5.4% yield, and the buyback retires about 2.5% of the shares each year. Together these make an 8% cash yield, which grows about 7% a year once capital spending falls from 2028. EPS grows about 4.4% a year from FY2026 to FY2030, roughly 60% of it from the falling share count, on EBITDA growing only 1.1% to 1.6% a year.

OTE is a cash distributor: an 8% cash yield that grows about 7% a year, on EBITDA growing under 2% a year.

The cash leg makes the return skew unusually benign: a bad multiple outcome breaks even, and a good multiple outcome pays 30% to 50%. At the guideline fair multiple of 12.5x, the model gives +36% over 18 months: 11 points from dividends, 8 points from earnings growth and 16 points from re-rating. The dividend and earnings legs (about 19% in total, 13% annualised) are high-probability mechanics. The re-rating leg is the swing, and it is a judgement about Greece (the spring 2027 election, the MSCI index transition in May 2027, the sovereign) and about two OTE decisions, not about European telecoms: the sector basket explains only 2% of OTE's daily share-price variance.

My fair multiple is 11.8x, OTE's ten-year median, which gives about +29% over 18 months. At an unchanged multiple of 10.8x the 18-month return is still about +19%. At OTE's ten-year 10th-percentile multiple of 8.7x, the 18-month return is roughly zero.

The investment case turns on one decision over 18 months and on two decisions over four years. The first decision is the inflation-linked price step on about two million postpaid contracts in early 2027. That price step supplies almost all of FY2027's net EBITDA growth (about EUR 21m); each point of price step is worth EUR 7m to 9m of EBITDA, or EUR 0.016 of EPS, and the outcome will be known within about twelve weeks. The second decision joins from 2028: how fast Vodafone, and possibly Nova, move wholesale lines from OTE's network to the Vodafone-PPC fibre venture. OTE's national wholesale revenue is about EUR 227m at an 80% to 85% margin. The price step and the wholesale migration roughly cancel in FY2028, which makes FY2028 the weakest and least predictable operating year and the year where consensus (EPS +7.1%) is most exposed.

I expect neither an upgrade cycle nor a reset. Consensus is right on 18-month EPS. Consensus is about 5% too high on FY2027 revenue, because several brokers have not removed the guided EUR 130m of zero-margin transit revenue; 2% to 4% too high on FY2028 to FY2029 EPS; and 4% to 6% too low on the dividend. Management has never missed a numerical EBITDAaL target and has never raised one in-year. The 25 February 2027 results will most likely bring an "about +2%" EBITDAaL guide, a cut to revenue consensus, a dividend raise and a confirmed FY2026. The dashboard grades sell-side momentum D and technical momentum B, and both grades are right.

Where I differ from the market, in five lines.
  1. 1The lead broker frames the Vodafone-PPC venture as easing retail overbuild; I read the venture as PPC's attack moving from retail, where PPC failed, to wholesale, where PPC now has an anchor tenant.
  2. 2The market treats the early-2027 price step as one input to "3% mobile growth"; I see the price step as binary, political (the election falls in May to July 2027) and the whole of FY2027's growth.
  3. 3Consensus FY2028 EPS growth of +7.1% on EBITDA growth of +1.7% contradicts consensus's own arithmetic.
  4. 4Consensus has not applied the dividend formula: the FY2026 dividend should be EUR 1.02, not EUR 0.96, with a 15% to 20% chance of EUR 1.30 if the EUR 170m tax windfall is passed through.
  5. 5The European telecom sector's rate-driven de-rating is not OTE's problem, and a sector recovery is not OTE's opportunity.
What to watch, in date order
  1. December 2026 Tariff schedules: the size of the early-2027 price step (a full 4% step is the upside branch; no step costs about 3% of FY2027 EPS).
  2. 25 February 2027 FY2027 EBITDAaL guide ("about +2%" is my central case) and the FY2026 distribution (EUR 1.02 dividend, or more if the tax windfall is passed through).
  3. Late April 2027 MSCI pricing window for Greece's move to developed-market status.
  4. May to July 2027 Greek national election; first-quarter 2027 print (revenue about -7%, expected and not a warning).
  5. Every quarter National wholesale revenue (about EUR 57m a quarter): a year-on-year fall above 8% to 10% signals fast migration to the Vodafone-PPC venture.

The four judgements that move the shares most, with the arithmetic

Every operating judgement converts to EPS by simple arithmetic, because everything below EBITDA is mechanical. Depreciation and amortisation are flat at about EUR 590m, the debt is fixed-rate, the tax rate is 23.5% and the buyback is formulaic. An EBITDA change therefore moves EPS by 76.5% of the change, divided by the year's average share count (381.6m shares in FY2027, 372.0m in FY2028 and 362.6m in FY2029). On the valuation side, one turn of the two-year-forward P/E is worth about EUR 1.88 a share at the 18-month horizon, or 10% of today's price.

Judgement 1. The early-2027 price step decides FY2027.

The model assumes an effective price step of about 3%: a 3.5% to 4% step, weighted for the probability that the step is capped or not applied. That effective step adds EUR 24m to FY2027 EBITDA, and each point of step is worth EUR 7m to 9m.

  • No step in 2027 (I put this at 20% to 25%, up from the second set's 15% to 20%, because of the election): EBITDA -EUR 24m → net income -EUR 18.4m → EPS -EUR 0.048 → FY2027 EPS EUR 1.64 (-2.8%). FY2027 EBITDA growth falls to about 0%; the February guide reads "about +1%" or is qualitative; consensus FY2027 EBITDA falls 2% to 3%. If the step is never applied, FY2028 EPS also loses about EUR 0.09 (EUR 1.76 → EUR 1.67, -5%).
  • Step delayed past the election to mid-year (about 25%): a half-year effect of about +EUR 14m instead of +EUR 24m → EPS -EUR 0.02 → FY2027 EPS EUR 1.67.
  • Full 4% step from January on mobile and fixed (50% to 55%): +EUR 31m, which is EUR 7m above the model → EPS +EUR 0.014 → FY2027 EPS EUR 1.70. The guide reads "about +3%"; consensus EBITDA rises about 1% and consensus EPS about 2%.
  • Effect on value: the price step's EPS swing is small (-3% to +1%), but the price step also sets the February guide and the market narrative. The bad branch plausibly costs 0.5x to 1.0x of multiple (5% to 10% of the share price) on top of the EPS loss; the good branch adds 2% to 5%. The outcome is observable within weeks in the tariff schedules and is confirmed by first-quarter 2027 mobile service revenue growth (a jump from about 2% to 3.5% to 4%).

Judgement 2. The speed of wholesale migration decides FY2028 to FY2030, and its risk is skewed to the downside.

The model has national wholesale revenue falling from EUR 227m in FY2026 to EUR 156m in FY2030, which costs EUR 13m, EUR 18m, EUR 16m and EUR 14m of EBITDA in successive years.

  • Fast tail (10% to 15%): Nova is sold to a buyer that joins the Vodafone-PPC venture, and both rivals migrate their lines within two to three years, costing a further EUR 60m to 100m of EBITDA. At FY2029, -EUR 60m of EBITDA → EPS -EUR 0.13 → EUR 1.71 (-7%); -EUR 100m → EPS -EUR 0.21 → EUR 1.63 (-11.5%). OTE has no second segment or geography to absorb that loss.
  • Slow case (about 25%): volume commitments and in-building cabling hold wholesale erosion at the FY2025 pace (about EUR 15m of revenue a year). EBITDA is then about EUR 6m better than the model in FY2028 (+EUR 0.012 of EPS) and about EUR 15m better by FY2030.
  • How to track it: quarterly national wholesale revenue (about EUR 57m now; a year-on-year fall above 8% to 10% signals acceleration); the venture's closing and any competition remedies (first half of 2027); and the identity of Nova's buyer.
The wholesale risk is skewed to the downside: the fast tail costs up to 11.5% of FY2029 EPS, while the slow case adds under 1%.

Judgement 3. The multiple Greece pays is the largest judgement for value, not for EPS.

Two-year-forward EPS at the 18-month horizon is about EUR 1.88 (the model's +7.8%). At 12.5x that gives a share price of EUR 23.5 before dividends (+36% total return); at 11.8x, EUR 22.2 (+29%); at an unchanged 10.8x, EUR 20.2 (+19%); at 9.5x, EUR 17.8 (+6%); and at 8.7x, EUR 16.3 (-2%). The drivers of the multiple are dated: the price step and the guide (February 2027); the MSCI pricing window (late April 2027, where net passive inflow is only about USD 63m against heavy active emerging-market ownership); the election (May to July 2027); and the clearance of the Vodafone-PPC venture.

Judgement 4. The February 2027 distribution decision carries upside now and a headline risk a year later.

FY2026 reported free cash flow of about EUR 745m includes about EUR 170m of one-off tax cash from the Romanian exit. The model assumes a EUR 590m distribution (a dividend of EUR 1.02 a share plus a EUR 186m buyback) and assumes that most of the windfall is held against the 2027 spectrum payment, as the chief executive said in November 2025.

  • Full pass-through of the windfall (15% to 20%): an extra EUR 155m. Paid as dividend, it adds EUR 0.40 a share (a dividend of about EUR 1.42, 2% of the share price in cash). Spent on buyback, it retires about 7.8m shares at EUR 20, 2.0% of the count, and lifts EPS by 2% in every future year (FY2027 EPS EUR 1.69 → EUR 1.72).
  • The reverse risk, a year later: applying the payout formula mechanically to FY2027 free cash flow after spectrum (EUR 516m) would give a 2028 dividend of about EUR 0.92, against the model's EUR 1.07. I expect management to smooth the dividend, but I put a 30% risk on a disappointing headline.
The distribution decision carries its upside in February 2027 and its headline risk a year later.

Several items look large and barely move EPS; the one item that would move EPS a lot is in no one's model. A 10% miss in System Solutions revenue, a EUR 130m transit exit and a EUR 30m "creep" in depreciation and amortisation each move EPS by pennies or not at all; the second set of inputs disproved the depreciation creep that the first set feared, using FactSet's flat quarterly series. Releveraging to 1.5x EBITDA would retire about a quarter of the shares and add about 23% to EPS, but Deutsche Telekom calls releveraging unpalatable, so it is a right tail with a probability under 5%.

#1 The operating environment: tailwinds, headwinds and the absence of risk

Judgement: the operating environment is a slight net negative for earnings over 18 months and mildly negative beyond, and the external forces acting on OTE's share price are larger than those acting on its earnings.

Demand is structurally stable in units, rising in value and highly visible. Broadband lines (2.37m) fall 0.4% a year and fixed lines 1.1% a year, but fibre is now 31% of the broadband base (21% a year ago) and earns about 10% more per line. 55% of Greek mobile lines are still prepaid, against over 75% postpaid in Western Europe, and each prepaid-to-postpaid migration adds EUR 3 to 5 a month. Pay-TV grows 6% to 8% a year, helped by curbs on content sharing and EUR 750 fines for piracy. Greek GDP grows about 2% a year, against 0.3% to 1.0% for the euro area.

Publicly funded information and communication technology (ICT) work is the one cyclical swing in demand. OTE's System Solutions revenue grew 76% in the first quarter of 2026 and 9% in the third quarter, as the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility winds down (it ends in December 2026). The downturn should be shallower than the boom, because only about 56% of the grants will have been absorbed by end-2026, public spending lags by about two years and a EUR 515m electronic-ID tender is pending. Even so, the first half of 2027 laps growth of +76% and +52%.

Regulation is unusually favourable today, but every protection is state-granted and three decisions fall in the next six months. The favourable rules are a copper stop-sell wherever fibre exists, relief from margin-squeeze tests on fibre, a wholesale volume-discount scheme (up to 28%) approved by EETT (the Greek telecom regulator) and the European Commission that locks Vodafone and Nova in, the removal of the pay-TV and broadband taxes, and a 2027 spectrum renewal at about EUR 78m, against EUR 119m fifteen years ago, on longer terms. The known negatives are already in guidance: a proposed 10% to 13% cut in OTE's fibre wholesale price, partly offset by a 4% to 5% rise in copper wholesale prices. The three pending decisions are the final wholesale price (under Commission review), the Competition Commission's view of the Vodafone-PPC venture, and political tolerance of a price step by the former state operator, with headline inflation at 5.6% a few months before a national election.

Competition has changed shape rather than intensity: PPC's retail attack failed, but PPC's network has now found a wholesale anchor tenant. PPC sold fibre at EUR 17.90 a month, 50% to 59% below the incumbents, and won under 20,000 customers in a year, because 70% of OTE's broadband customers bundle mobile and PPC has no mobile, TV or telecom brand. PPC's aerial fibre network, however, passes 2.3m homes at about EUR 160 a home, against about EUR 500 a line for OTE. In August 2026 Vodafone Greece (0.91m broadband customers) and PPC signed a term sheet for a 50:50 wholesale venture covering 1.6m homes, targeting 3.8m by 2028 and closing in the first half of 2027. The first evidence has reached OTE's numbers: retail fixed service revenue fell 0.6% in the third quarter despite a record 52,000 fibre additions, OTE is re-contracting customers in PPC's areas, and OTE lost 8,164 broadband customers in one quarter. Mobile competition remains rational: Vodafone and Nova raised prices with inflation two years running, and PPC rules out entering mobile.

Costs add modest pressure, and the loss of Champions League rights trades a content saving for a retention risk. Energy hedge cover falls from 80% in 2026 to 66% in 2027, and wages drift up 3% to 4% on EUR 365m of personnel cost. The UEFA club-competition rights went to SPOR FM TV for about EUR 330m (the market expected EUR 200m), so OTE's Magenta TV loses the Champions League from August 2027 unless it sub-licenses the rights. That loss saves content cost but puts 802,000 pay-TV subscribers at risk.

Macro conditions reach OTE's earnings barely, but reach its multiple heavily. OTE's debt is fixed-rate and in euros, and 99.9% of its revenue is in euros. Telecoms, however, trade as yield stocks, and the US ten-year yield is above 5%. Pulling the other way are Greece's reclassification to developed-market status (FTSE and STOXX are done; MSCI follows in May 2027) and a lower Greek risk premium.

Where I differ from the market. The consensus narrative treats the Vodafone-PPC venture as consolidation that eases fears of fibre overbuild (Morgan Stanley, September 2026). I think that reading is exactly backwards for OTE's wholesale line: a failed retail entrant has become a funded wholesale platform with a captive anchor tenant. European precedent (Open Fiber against Telecom Italia; SIRO against eir; alternative networks against Openreach) says the incumbent keeps its retail customers and loses wholesale lines over three to five years. I agree with the market that a retail price war is very unlikely within 18 months, because OTE's rivals cannot fund one.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case has four parts: the Vodafone-PPC venture closes slowly (the Belgian precedent took over a year); the volume commitments bind for longer than I assume; Nova's buyer is a leveraged financial owner who stays on OTE's discounted wholesale terms; and the price step is applied in full, because the ruling party is 10 points ahead and voters see inflation as a reason for indexation rather than against it. I would turn more positive if the venture's clearance carried open-access price remedies, if Vodafone said publicly that its migration is geographically constrained, or if national wholesale erosion stayed under 6% a year through 2027.
Conclusion: the environment protects OTE's retail franchise and margins but offers no growth tailwind; the near-term external positive is a single political decision (the price step), and the medium-term negative is a single competitor's migration speed.
Score: 46, set by the Rater. Demand is stable in units and rising in value (fibre 31% of the base, prepaid-to-postpaid migration, Greek GDP about 2%) and regulation is unusually favourable, but the external balance tips slightly negative: the Vodafone-PPC wholesale venture attacks a EUR 227m line at an 80-85% margin from 2027, public ICT laps +76% as the EU facility ends, UEFA rights are lost and energy cover falls; consensus sales growth at the 6th percentile overstates the damage because transit is zero-margin. Per Richard's ruling this sits above 40 and below internal forces, in the 40s (a C- or D, not an F), coherent with the group's 47.

#2 Internally driven change: strong, improving, and the absence of problems

Judgement: OTE's corporate change programme was strong, broad and well resourced, but it is 28 months old and has reached full output; what remains is a gentle positive (cost-out, the buyback and a latent price lever), with no new catalyst announced.

Kostas Nebis's programme has been delivered and is visible in the numbers. Mr Nebis has been Chairman and CEO since July 2024, having come from Deutsche Telekom's Croatian unit. Since then OTE has:

  • replaced the chief technology officer and chief information officer at once;
  • sold Telekom Romania, a 12%-margin unit that drained about EUR 70m of cash a year, and paid out the proceeds within three months;
  • exited about EUR 300m of zero-margin transit revenue;
  • launched fixed wireless access (134,000 customers, +116%) to contain Starlink;
  • taken over the Terna rural fibre concession for minimal consideration;
  • broken a multi-year price freeze with a 2.6% indexation step in December 2025, which was followed by a 17-year high in postpaid additions;
  • set its first explicit EBITDAaL guide (+3%, above the then consensus of +2.4%) and codified a 70% to 100% payout.

As a result, indirect costs fell from 31% to 28% of service revenue, the EBITDAaL margin rose from 38.2% (FY2024) to 42.1% (third quarter of 2026), and S&P upgraded OTE to A-.

Four parts of the programme are still working. First, net cost-out of about EUR 5m to 9m a year after inflation (EUR 25m to 30m gross): the 2026 voluntary-leave scheme, the largest in years, pays back in 2027, and copper switch-off starts in 2028. Second, a buyback funded by the payout rule. Third, capital spending guided at about EUR 600m a year to 2028 and towards EUR 550m by 2029, which adds about EUR 60m of free cash flow by 2030. Fourth, the price-indexation clause. In July 2026 OTE rewrote two million contracts to allow indexation "at the start of each year"; a company does not rewrite its contracts to leave such an option unused, so the rewrite reveals intent.

Three things are missing: numbered mid-term targets, any decision on the balance sheet or the 3,800 owned towers, and a growth lever. I put a capital markets day at about a one-in-four chance. The "Flywheel", "OTE 2030" and "AI-native" language, and the switch from the Cosmote brand to the Telekom brand in September 2026, are presentational and carry no line in the forecast.

OTE's problems are small but form a pattern.

  • Core service growth is slowing: mobile service revenue grew +5.5%, +2.3% and +2.0% through 2026 as the 2025 price moves lapped, and retail fixed revenue fell to -0.6%.
  • Growth quality has leaned on public ICT work at a 20% margin.
  • Adjusted EBITDAaL excludes voluntary-leave costs every year (EUR 31.5m in the first nine months of 2026, about EUR 0.06 to 0.08 of EPS) while keeping the savings those schemes produce.
  • In the third quarter OTE switched its fibre footprint definition from active-line availability (2.3m homes) to all homes passed (3.0m), which makes utilisation look lower (32% against 44%).
  • Governance meets only a controlled subsidiary's minimum: the Chairman and CEO roles are combined, three of ten directors are independent, all board terms expire together in 2027, related-party purchases total EUR 572m, and insiders hold almost no shares.
  • Deutsche Telekom does not participate in the buybacks, so its stake creeps up about 1.3 to 1.5 points a year towards 60% by 2030, while the free float (about 36.6%) shrinks. That slow loop favours the parent and cheapens any eventual buyout of minority shareholders.
The programme lifted the margin by almost four points, but core service growth has slowed through 2026 and the parent's stake creeps up.

Where I differ from the market. The market credits OTE's management as a value creator; I credit it as an honest tracker that delivers budgets and will not over-reach. That trait is a strength for predictability and a weakness for an investment case that needs acceleration. On the presentational points (the excluded voluntary-leave costs and the footprint redefinition) I am more cautious than the published research, which does not mention them.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that Deutsche Telekom's October 2026 artificial-intelligence programme reaches OTE's cost base faster than I model (a further EUR 10m to 15m of savings a year), that copper switch-off savings arrive two years early, or that a capital markets day in 2027 puts numbers on the Flywheel strategy. Any of a numbered EBITDAaL ambition above 3% a year, a tower monetisation, or a statement that the tax windfall will be fully distributed would move this topic up a grade.
Conclusion: the internal change programme is delivered and visible in the numbers; what remains is modest, mechanical and reliable, and no new internal catalyst is on the horizon.
Score: 58, set by the Rater. The Nebis programme (Romania sold, EUR 300m transit exited, first explicit guide, codified 70-100% payout, margin 38.2% to 42.1%) was strong but is 28 months old and at full output; what remains is net cost-out of EUR 5-9m a year, a payout-funded buyback adding about 2.6 points of EPS growth, the indexation clause and capex falling towards EUR 550m, offset by small patterned problems (slowing core service growth, voluntary-leave costs excluded from adjusted figures, a footprint redefinition, thin minority governance). Per Richard's ruling this is a gentle positive in the C band and not negative, just above his CVS Group 55 for mediocre gently positive change and a little below the group's 60 because no new catalyst is announced.

#3 Industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Judgement: OTE has among the most favourable industry structures in European telecoms, a moat that secures margins and cash rather than growth, the strongest financial profile in its peer set on every measure except growth, and a capable management team bounded by its parent's frame.

The Greek market's profits are far more concentrated than its market shares, and that concentration makes OTE's rivals price rationally. Three operators hold essentially all subscribers: OTE has 54% of broadband, 52% to 54% of mobile and about 80% of active fibre lines. In FY2024 OTE Greece generated EUR 784m of EBITDAaL less capital expenditure, against EUR 41m for Vodafone Greece and -EUR 33m for Nova. Nova's owner, United Group, carries 4.2x leverage and is selling Nova. OTE's rivals therefore price with inflation rather than for market share, and they rent OTE's network for 48% of their fibre customers. The market also has cooperative structures: territorially divided fibre builds, reciprocal sports content and volume-committed wholesale. When Nova cut retail prices by up to 50% in early 2023, Nova reversed the cuts within months. The one fragile layer is national wholesale, about 15% of OTE's EBITDA.

OTE's moats are stacked and mostly widening at retail and network level; the one narrowing moat is OTE's role as wholesale host. The retail and network moats are ownership of ducts OTE need not share, the only 5G Stand-Alone network (85% population coverage), 70% to 71% of customers on converged bundles, ten years of Ookla fastest-network awards and the cheapest capital in the market. State-granted protections are strong but revocable. The proof that OTE's offer is not inferior is strong: a 50% to 59% cheaper offer failed.

The constraint on OTE is the size of its field, not the strength of its moat. Greek telecom revenue is about EUR 5bn, growing 2% to 4% a year in nominal terms, and two-thirds of it is already OTE's. OTE's dominance closes off in-market acquisitions, and OTE's strategy closes off expansion into other countries.

Against the four peers in the files, OTE has the strongest financial profile on every measure except revenue growth.

OTE's earnings engine has changed: falling depreciation drove past profit growth, and from here EBITDA has to do the work. Return on equity is 29%, and cash conversion on the company's definition is 85% to 95% of adjusted net income. From 2019 to 2025 EBIT rose from EUR 272m to EUR 849m because depreciation and amortisation halved (from EUR 1,138m to EUR 582m) and interest costs fell. That depreciation-led engine is now spent.

Management is capable and reliable, but not outstanding. The team is fast on the decisions available to it, has never missed a numerical EBITDAaL target (including through the 2022 to 2023 energy shock), and is paid on EBITDAaL, free cash flow and return on capital. The team has no beat-and-raise culture, is evasive on the medium term, and discloses no segment margins, average revenue per user or churn; peers Telekom Austria, Orange Polska and Magyar Telekom all quantify their indexation, and OTE does not. The CFO has served since 2012 and has no tested successor. Capital allocation is disciplined and formulaic rather than enlightened: the exits were excellent, but the buybacks are price-insensitive and the balance sheet is idle.

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the sell-side on OTE's quality and dominance. I weight two points more heavily than the sell-side does. First, OTE's moat protects a bounded field, which argues for a yield-stock multiple rather than a compounder's multiple. Second, OTE's governance (30% board independence, the parent's creeping stake, near-zero insider ownership) is a permanent and partly structural reason for a discount to independent peers.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The Greek market structure could prove more fragile than it looks if Nova's buyer is a strategic owner that joins the Vodafone-PPC venture, which would turn the "weak rivals" loop into a "funded rival platform" loop faster than I model, or if a bidder appeared for mobile spectrum at the 2027 renewal (a probability under 5%, but it would invert the thesis). A tower monetisation at the multiple Deutsche Telekom achieved for its own towers (25x EBITDAaL) would show that the parent's frame is less rigid than I assume.
Conclusion: OTE's foundations are top-decile in Europe; they make the cash dependable and the retail franchise safe, and they do nothing for growth.
Score: 76, set by the Rater. A three-player, rational market where OTE takes 93% of operating free cash flow, stacked moats proven by a half-price entrant winning under 1% of its base, and a top-decile profile (ROIC 25.8%, 94th percentile; EBITDA margin 41%, 83rd; 0.4x leverage; A-) under a capable but parent-bounded management; held back by a bounded Greek field growing 2-4% nominal, a narrowing wholesale moat, revocable state protections, weak minority governance and low returns on new capital (fibre earns low single digits until utilisation passes 50-60%, capex at 18% of revenue). Coherent with the groups (83, 72, 76, 64): clearly above Tenaris on structure and predictability, below Reply because new capital earns little.

#4 Guidance: conservatism, expectation management and the delivery record

Judgement: OTE's guidance is reliable rather than conservative; the company sets numbers it is sure of and confirms them four times a year, so the only question that matters is the level of the FY2027 guide on 25 February 2027, which I expect at or slightly below consensus.

The delivery record is clean: OTE lands what it guides, and has never raised guidance in-year under this chief executive. FY2025 EBITDAaL grew +2.0%, as guided. FY2026 was guided at about +3% in February 2026, above the then consensus, and is running at +3.0% after nine months; the fourth quarter needs about EUR 362m (+3%), and management holds EUR 10m to 15m of cost timing in reserve. Quarterly EBITDAaL in 2026 landed within -0.3% to +0.7% of consensus. Free cash flow guidance has been trimmed once in six years, by 2% in FY2024, for working capital.

The Magyar Telekom precedent is not a template for an in-year raise at OTE. Deutsche Telekom's other subsidiaries set guidance the same way, and Magyar Telekom raised in-year in May 2026. A sell-side report reads that raise as a template for OTE, but Magyar had already applied its 4.4% fee adjustment when it raised, while OTE's 2027 price step is still undecided.

Management lands what it guides and has never raised in-year: guidance is reliable, not conservative.

The arithmetic of the FY2027 guide is the arithmetic of the price step. On 30 October management signalled informally that 2027 would "stay within these kind of growth levels", with System Solutions at "more or less the same levels" and capital spending "a bit over" EUR 600m. That signal implies about +3% EBITDAaL growth, above the model (+1.5% EBITDAaL; +1.4% on the brokers' EBITDA basis) and in line with consensus (+2.5%). A full price step plus flat ICT revenue gives about +EUR 30m to 34m on EUR 1,416m, which management would round to "about +2%" or stretch to "+2% to +3%". An "about +3%" guide needs a 4% step on both mobile and fixed. No step gives growth of roughly zero.

My probabilities for the February guide favour "about +2%", so FY2027 consensus EBITDA is more likely to be trimmed than raised. I put "about +2%" at 40% to 45%, "about +3%" or "+2% to +3%" at 30% to 35%, and "+1% to +2%" or a qualitative guide at 25%. On the first and third outcomes, consensus FY2027 EBITDA is trimmed by half a point to a point; on the second, consensus holds or rises about 1%.

OTE manages expectations precisely on outputs and stays silent on building blocks. OTE is specific on EBITDAaL growth, capital spending, underlying and reported free cash flow, transit revenue by year and the payout formula. OTE says nothing on the size and cap of the price step, ICT margin and backlog, the wholesale trajectory or voluntary-exit savings. The reported free cash flow guide of about EUR 750m needs about EUR 400m in the fourth quarter, which invites a headline "miss" on tax or public-receipt timing even if underlying free cash flow of EUR 570m to 580m is met.

Where I differ from the market. Consensus anchors on guidance and sits at +2.5% EBITDAaL growth for FY2027. I sit a point below on EBITDA but in line on EPS, because I assume flat depreciation and a 23.5% tax rate against consensus's implied 24.4%. I am more cautious than management's informal signal, because management had not committed to the price step on 30 October and because the election makes a capped or delayed step more likely than it was in the summer. I am above consensus on the one guidance item that the payout formula makes visible a year ahead: the distribution.
Counter-case and what would change my view. If OTE announced a December price step of 3.5% or more on both mobile and fixed, the "about +3%" branch would become the most likely outcome and FY2027 consensus would move up, not down. A guide phrased "at least" for the first time would signal that management's culture has shifted from tracking to beating, and I would then re-rate this topic.
Conclusion: OTE's record says that whatever is guided will be met, but the level will be set at or a little below where the market already is, so guidance will not lead expectations upward in the next 18 months.
Score: 61, set by the Rater. Management has never missed a numerical EBITDAaL target (FY2025 +2.0% as guided, FY2026 +3% on track, quarterly EBITDAaL within -0.3% to +0.7% of consensus) with one 2% free-cash-flow trim in six years, and the FY2026 guide was set above consensus; but it has never raised in-year, is silent on building blocks, and the FY2027 guide will most likely land at or slightly below consensus, so guidance is reliable rather than conservative. A clean honest tracker without beat-and-raise sits above the group's 54 and Renew (which cut) and below MITIE's continuing upgrade record.

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Judgement: OTE's profit drop-through is exceptional, but the revenue it acts on is small; positive leverage (price) and negative leverage (wholesale) are now nearly matched, financial leverage is an unused option, and the loop that dominates per-share value is the capital-return loop.

OTE's pricing power is proven once in mobile and partly contradicted in fixed broadband. The 2.6% mobile step in December 2025 on about two million contracts is worth about EUR 20m to 24m a year at about a 95% margin, with no visible churn; the prepaid minimum top-up is EUR 13 to 15. In fixed broadband, the -0.6% third quarter and retention discounting in PPC's areas contradict that pricing power. The mechanism for recurring rises exists: the July 2026 indexation clause was written into contracts at signing, so the September 2026 European court ruling against discretionary clauses at Vodafone Germany should not reach it. Rivals provide cover, having raised prices twice each.

OTE's price rises are nominal catch-up, not real pricing power. Greek consumer prices outran telecom prices by 25% over four years. Once inflation falls, the durable form of price rise is a flat money increase (Orange Polska's PLN 5 a month), which OTE has not yet used.

Operating leverage is high on core services, which makes group revenue growth the wrong measure of OTE's progress. Between 61% and 66% of cash operating costs are fixed. A 1% rise in core service revenue (about EUR 22m across mobile service, retail fixed and national wholesale) adds about EUR 18m to 20m of EBITDA (1.3%) and about 2.1% to EPS. A 1% rise in cost inflation on EUR 1.1bn of controllable cost costs EUR 11m. Transit revenue carries no margin and ICT about 15%. FY2027 revenue therefore falls 4% while EBITDA rises about 1.4%. The margin rises from 40.5% (FY2025) to 45.2% (FY2030); about 3 points of that gain is mix and 1.5 points is genuine operating leverage.

The EBITDA bridge is the whole case in one chart: the price step is the only large positive, and wholesale erosion nearly cancels it in FY2028. Price adds EUR 20m to 24m a year and wholesale erosion costs EUR 13m to 18m a year, while volume and mix (+EUR 8m to 10m), net cost (+EUR 6m to 9m) and System Solutions (-EUR 6m to +EUR 1m) are small. The price step's value shrinks as Greek inflation falls towards 2.5% to 3%, while wholesale erosion peaks as the Vodafone-PPC venture fills. The two forces cross in FY2028, when net EBITDA growth dips to EUR 16m from EUR 21m.

Financial leverage is an unused option: OTE's balance sheet is nearly ungeared and stays that way under the payout policy. Net debt is EUR 683m (0.5x EBITDA including leases; 0.2x to 0.3x on brokers' definitions), all fixed-rate and in euros, with interest cover above 20x. The September 2026 refinancing (EUR 350m at 3.853%, replacing EUR 500m at 0.875%) costs about EUR 7m a year as a one-off step, or 1% of EPS. A 100 basis-point rise at the next refinancing would cost 0.4% of EPS. Leverage falls to about 0.25x and stays there, because distributions roughly equal free cash flow. The option to releverage to 1.5x, which would add 23% to EPS, is real but nobody has proposed it.

Six feedback loops act on OTE, and the capital-return loop dominates per-share value.

  1. Capital return (reinforcing and dominant): free cash flow funds buybacks whose shares are cancelled, raising cash and payouts per share by about 2.6 points of EPS growth a year.
  2. Fibre lock-in (mixed): the copper stop-sell, in-building cabling and bundles hold volume, but OTE is giving back price, so retail fixed revenue grows only +1.0% and then +0.5%.
  3. Weak rivals (positive, now reversing): the Vodafone-PPC venture is precisely a cash-constrained rival's answer to OTE's dominance, converting Vodafone's wholesale payments to OTE into equity in its own network.
  4. Venture utilisation (negative, building from 2027): an anchor tenant lowers the venture's unit cost and wholesale price and draws in the next tenant; Nova is the swing tenant.
  5. ICT boom and bust (balancing): small for EBITDA, but positive for cash as public receivables (EUR 716m at the first-quarter peak) are collected.
  6. Inflation and price (self-limiting): high inflation enlarges the price step, but also squeezes the prepaid base and raises political resistance.
One loop dominates per-share value, the capital return; the loop now turning against OTE is the rival venture's fill-up.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side discusses price as a steady support to "about 3% mobile service growth" and cost-out as a margin story. I would state both points more sharply. Without the price step, EBITDA is flat to slightly down in every forecast year. Cost-out is the stabiliser that lets management land guidance, not a growth engine. The leverage that matters for EPS is the falling share count, not gearing.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the regulator's proposed 10% to 13% cut in OTE's fibre wholesale price narrows the price gap the Vodafone-PPC venture can offer and so slows migration, a balancing loop that trades OTE's wholesale price for wholesale volume. Copper switch-off savings could also prove larger and earlier than the EUR 8m to 10m a year by 2030 that I assume. If Deutsche Telekom softened its stance on leverage (its 2027 finance strategy is the next review point), the grade of this whole topic would change.
Conclusion: revenue growth converts to profit at close to 100% on the lines that matter, but those lines grow about 1% a year and the two large forces (price and wholesale) offset, so OTE's leverage shows up as margin arithmetic and per-share mechanics rather than as outsized profit growth.
Score: 62, set by the Rater. The structure has real gearing: 61-66% of cash costs are fixed, price drops through at about 95% (the 2.6% step was worth EUR 20-24m) and 1% of core service revenue is about 2.1% of EPS, with a reinforcing capital-return loop (cancelled buybacks) and an unused leverage option (1.5x would add about 23% to EPS). But pricing is nominal catch-up proven once in mobile and contradicted in fixed, and negative leverage on high-margin wholesale and a filling rival venture now roughly match the positive, so the gears show up as margin mix and per-share mechanics rather than outsized profit growth; above the ordinary mix, below the 75 level of operating leverage proven in both directions.

#6 Forecast financials: scope for double-digit growth and for higher growth or margins than the past

Judgement: no earnings line grows at double digits; margins rise far above the past for mechanical reasons; EPS grows about 4.4% a year, more steadily and predictably than in the past but with lower operating quality; free cash flow per share and the dividend are the only lines that approach high-single-digit growth.

The forecast numbers are mostly arithmetic: transit and ICT drive revenue down, the price step drives EBITDA up, and the buyback drives EPS.

  • FY2026 is 91% delivered.
  • FY2027 revenue falls 4.1% because the last EUR 130m of zero-margin transit revenue goes and System Solutions revenue declines 7%, against management's "same levels". FY2027 EBITDA rises 1.4%, as set out in the bridge in #5. The margin gain is mix arithmetic.
  • Net income grows only 1.7% a year, because depreciation and amortisation stay flat and interest steps up once. FactSet's EBITDA less EBIT has been EUR 142m to 147m in every quarter since early 2025, and the renewed spectrum amortises at roughly half the old rate.
  • EPS grows 19% from FY2026 to FY2030: 10.7 points from the falling share count and 7.2 points from net income.
  • Free cash flow dips 10% in FY2027, because cash tax normalises (from about EUR 51m to EUR 155m to 170m once the Romanian-exit benefit has arrived) and about EUR 78m of spectrum is paid. Free cash flow per share then grows about 7% a year, as capital spending falls from EUR 620m before spectrum to EUR 540m and ICT receivables are released.
  • Reported EPS will run EUR 0.06 to 0.08 below adjusted EPS every year, because of voluntary-leave cash costs.

The first half of 2027 will read like a stall even if the full year is on track. In the first quarter of 2027, revenue falls about 7% and EBITDA grows only about +0.5% to +1%, because ICT revenue laps +76% growth and the price step is only partly in. EBITDA growth in the second half runs at about +2%.

Where I differ from the market. On revenue, I am about 5% below consensus in FY2027 for bookkeeping reasons: brokers' FY2027 revenue forecasts span EUR 3,383m to 3,613m, and Morgan Stanley, Wood, Alpha Finance and Goldman Sachs have not removed transit. On EBITDA, I am 1% to 2% below consensus in FY2027 to FY2029. On EPS, I am in line with consensus for 18 months and 2% to 4% below after that, because consensus FY2028 EPS growth of +7.1% needs 4% to 5% net income growth that nothing in the drivers supplies. On the dividend, I am 4% to 6% above consensus, because consensus has not applied the payout formula.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The upper end of the FY2027 range is EBITDA of EUR 1,492m (+3%) and EPS of EUR 1.74 to 1.75, which needs a 4% price step from January and flat ICT revenue. The lower end is EBITDA of EUR 1,435m to 1,445m and EPS of EUR 1.62 to 1.64, with no price step and ICT revenue down 15%. For FY2028 to FY2030 the downside tail is longer than the upside tail. I would raise the out-year forecasts on a capital decision (a tower sale, releveraging or a full pass-through of the tax windfall), and on nothing operational.
Conclusion: the forecasts describe one of the most predictable earnings streams in European telecoms and one of the slowest: EBITDA grows 1% to 2% a year, EPS 4% to 5%, and free cash flow per share and the dividend about 7%, with no double-digit line and no acceleration.
Score: 37, set by the Rater. Growth of 0-5% gives D; I place it in the upper half of the band because the margin path (40.5% to 45.2%) is far above the past and the EPS line is highly predictable, but not higher because about 60% of the growth is share count on net income growing only 1.7% a year, revenue falls 0.5% a year and the margin gain is mostly mix from exiting zero-margin transit, consistent with the Financial forecasts group's 30 and the earlier 36.

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Judgement: the base case has no upgrade cycle (about a one-in-four chance of a mild one); it has a near-certain dividend upgrade, a revenue cut that screens badly and means nothing, and a market narrative that knows every fact and has done none of the arithmetic.

I expect favourable revisions first and adverse revisions a year later.

  • 25 February 2027: FY2026 is met. FY2027 revenue consensus is cut by EUR 100m to 170m as transit is removed. FY2027 EBITDA consensus is trimmed 0.5% to 1% on an "about +2%" guide (about 60% likely), held (25%) or lifted 1% (15% to 20%). FY2027 EPS consensus holds within 1%. The FY2026 dividend is raised 4% to 6% against consensus, or by about 35% if the tax windfall is passed through.
  • May and July 2027: two quarters print revenue down 5% to 7% and EBITDA up only 0.5% to 1.5%, during and after the election, so brokers trim the first half and hold the full year. National wholesale is the line to watch.
  • November 2027: second-half EBITDA growth of about +2% restores the year; this is the first possible small upgrade, if the price step was applied in full.
  • February 2028: the FY2028 guide ("about +1%" to "+2%") lands below consensus EBITDA growth (+1.7%) and EPS growth (+7.1%), and FY2028 EPS consensus is cut 2% to 4%.

In EPS terms the upgrade and downgrade cases are nearly symmetric (+3% against -4%); in optics the balance is negative, because the only line revised up is the dividend, and revision screens do not weigh dividends. The upgrade case (20% to 25%) needs a 4% price step in January on mobile and fixed, flat ICT revenue and an "about +3%" guide confirmed through the year. The downgrade case (25% to 30%) is no price step or a post-election step, ICT revenue down 15% in the first half, and the Vodafone-PPC venture closing with a Vodafone migration timetable.

In EPS the upgrade and downgrade cases are nearly symmetric (+3% against -4%); in optics the balance is negative.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side report in the files expects "consensus revisions to shift decisively higher" after February, on the strength of management's informal signal. I do not, because the arithmetic of the price step against wholesale erosion does not support a decisive move in either direction. I agree that the market has no new fact to learn; what it lacks is the arithmetic.
Counter-case and what would change my view. A December tariff announcement of 3.5% or more on both mobile and fixed, plus a stated intention to distribute the tax windfall, would lift the upgrade case above 40%, and I would move this topic to constructive. Conversely, a first-quarter national wholesale print down more than 8% would start the FY2028 consensus cuts early.
Conclusion: the next six to twelve months bring a dividend upgrade and a revenue downgrade that cancel in the headlines, an EPS consensus that barely moves, and a market narrative that can only improve by doing arithmetic it has so far declined to do.

#8 Current momentum: guidance, estimates, narrative, price, and peers

Judgement: price momentum is positive but fading, estimate momentum is flat to negative, narrative momentum has turned cautious in ratings rather than in numbers, and the stock has decoupled from a sector in retreat.

Guidance momentum is neutral. Guidance has been reiterated four times and never raised; the one positive surprise was the February 2026 guide, set above consensus.

Estimate momentum has stalled, and ratings are drifting down while the numbers hold. FactSet consensus for FY2027 has barely moved: EPS changed 0%, +1%, -1% and +1% over one, three, six and twelve months; EBITDA 0%, 0%, -1% and +1%; and sales 0%, 0%, 0% and -4% (the -4% is transit). The target price changed 0%, 0% and +4% over one, three and six months. The share of Buy ratings is 54%, down 8 points in three months and 15 points in six; the revision-momentum score is -2, and the dashboard's sell-side momentum grade is D. Brokers' moves after the third-quarter results were small: Morgan Stanley cut FY2027 EPS from EUR 1.68 to EUR 1.67, and Barclays cut FY2027 EBITDAaL by 0.6%.

The brokers disagree on value, not on earnings: targets range from EUR 17.50 to EUR 23.80, and the mean target of EUR 20.88 is 11% above the share price. Morgan Stanley rates OTE Buy at EUR 23.80, calling it "a new OTE" with an 8.5% unlevered free cash flow yield against 6% for the sector. Barclays rates it Sell at EUR 18.00 on a sector thesis (artificial-intelligence switching agents and satellites). Goldman Sachs (EUR 19.50), Eurobank (EUR 17.50) and New Street (EUR 21.20) rate it Hold. Deutsche Bank, the most bullish published voice (Buy, EUR 23), has shown no rating since 23 October, most likely because of a restriction.

Price momentum is positive but fading: the dashboard grades it B. The share price is up 20% over twelve months and 22% over nine, but only 8% over six and down 4.5% over three. The price sits 3.8% above a 200-day moving average that has risen for twelve consecutive months, but below the 50-day average (EUR 19.46). The relative-strength percentile is 59, and the 52-week range is EUR 14.67 to EUR 20.48. Since end-July OTE has lagged Greek stocks by 9%. The two-year-forward P/E sits at the 58th percentile of its five-year range (9.1x to 14.0x) and at about the 40th percentile of its ten-year range.

OTE has decoupled from a European telecom sector in retreat. Since 19 May 2026 the sector has fallen 14% relative to the market, a de-rating (the median two-year-forward P/E fell 12%) on unchanged earnings. The dashboard's "Fitness for Fighting" market regime is bearish with high conviction, its Telecoms view is Neutral, and its Thematic Momentum grade is D. Over the latest six months the peer basket explains only 2% of OTE's daily share-price variance (beta 0.21), and OTE returned +7.9% while the basket fell 4.4%.

Orange Polska is the one peer that shows what a Deutsche Telekom-style incumbent looks like when it has a real change force. Among the named peers, only Orange Polska has both price and estimate momentum (B and B; +89% over twelve months; 16x two-year-forward P/E), on a case built on contractual price rises, deregulation and twice-raised targets. Telekom Austria (D and C, 8.1x) and Magyar Telekom (C, 9.4x) are flat; Cyfrowy Polsat is D and D; Deutsche Telekom itself is graded F on price.

The multiple is Greek, not sectoral: the sector explains 2% of OTE's daily moves, and OTE rose while the sector de-rated.

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard's letters are right, and I would not argue with either: B for price, D for estimates. What I add is that OTE's price momentum is Greek (the reclassification, a lower risk premium and the clearing of the PPC fear) rather than sectoral. The sector's bearish regime is therefore not a reason to expect OTE to fall, and a sector rally is not a reason to expect OTE to rise.
Counter-case and what would change my view. If sector theses like Barclays' keep reaching OTE's targets through lower terminal-growth assumptions, ratings could keep drifting down with no change in earnings; that is a sentiment risk rather than a fundamental one. A break above the 50-day average ahead of the December tariff announcements would restore the technical grade; a close below the 200-day average (about EUR 18.10) would end the twelve-month uptrend.
Conclusion: momentum is mixed in an informative way: the share price has risen on Greece and cash while estimates and ratings have gone nowhere, and nothing before 25 February 2027 is likely to change either reading.
Score: 54, set by the Rater. One measure negative and one positive gives C. Guidance was held four times (positive only in being set above consensus in February), FY2027 EPS revisions are flat (0%/+1%/-1%), buy share is down 15 points in six months, and the price is below its 50-day but 3.8% above a 200-day average rising for twelve months; peers are weak but not comparable drivers (2% of variance), so they do not move it, and I place it in the lower part of the band because the parts lean negative without strongly contradicting the measures.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

Judgement: the fundamental case is simple and low-risk, among the simplest in the cohort; the share-price risk is several times larger than the earnings risk and is driven by variables outside the earnings forecast.

OTE's forecast needs only strengths OTE has already shown, plus one habit shown once. OTE has one country, one currency, fixed-rate debt, no minorities or associates, a formulaic payout and a management team that lands what it guides. Three-quarters of the FY2027 EBITDA base is already visible. The forecast rests on four demonstrated strengths (landing guided EBITDAaL, taking out cost faster than inflation adds it, converting cash into a buyback, and holding retail share), on one habit demonstrated once (annual indexation), and on managing a wholesale loss that every precedent says is gradual. The forecast needs no strength the business lacks.

The forecast needs only strengths OTE has shown, plus one habit shown once.
The forecast needs
  • Landing guided EBITDAaL
  • Taking cost out faster than inflation adds it
  • Converting cash into a buyback
  • Holding retail share
  • Annual indexation (shown once)
  • Managing a gradual wholesale loss
It does not need
  • ICT growth
  • A tower sale
  • Releveraging
  • A retail share gain
  • A new product

The earnings range is narrow and slightly negatively skewed; the share-price range is about four times wider. FY2027 EBITDA ranges from EUR 1,435m to 1,492m (-1% to +3%) and EPS from EUR 1.62 to 1.75, with a 70% to 75% probability of landing within 2% to 4% of the base case. The skew is slightly negative, from the election, the UEFA loss and Nova's base shrinking 7% a year. FY2028 EBITDA ranges from EUR 1,410m to 1,525m, with a clearly longer downside tail. On today's two-year-forward EPS, the share price ranges from EUR 15.5 (8.7x) to EUR 22.3 (12.5x), or -17% to +19% before the 8% cash yield: about four times the EPS range. Over the last year the shares moved plus or minus 16% on a 4% move in consensus EPS.

OTE's fragilities are either small or unlikely; the most likely, a political block on the price step, costs about 3% of FY2027 EPS. The regulator could revisit the volume-discount scheme if rivals allege foreclosure; the UK precedent is Ofcom blocking an Openreach discount in September 2026. PPC could bid for mobile spectrum at the 2027 renewal, despite repeated denials. And an untested Greek rule on termination fees may let indexed customers leave without penalty when the price step applies, a hypothesis to test against first-quarter 2027 churn.

The fundamental risks are trackable; the sentiment risks are more sudden and more likely. The price step is observable within weeks and then in the first-quarter mobile service line. National wholesale revenue is disclosed quarterly, and management states the national figure on calls. The Vodafone-PPC venture's progress appears in PPC's, Vodafone's and the Competition Commission's filings. Retail fixed pricing, the ICT pipeline and pay-TV economics after the UEFA loss cannot be monitored, because OTE discloses no average revenue per user, churn, backlog, segment margins or clause terms.

A 10% to 15% share-price fall with no change in the company is plausible within 18 months. Five sentiment risks could cause it:

  • interest rates, because telecoms trade as yield stocks;
  • sector theses priced into OTE's targets through terminal growth;
  • the MSCI transition, because active emerging-market funds hold Greece as their second-largest overweight and may sell more than developed-market passive funds buy (Greece underperformed for 10 to 11 months after its 2001 upgrade);
  • a free float of about 36.6% that trades only EUR 9m to 12m a day;
  • sales-revision screens that read the transit exit as downgrades.

At trough multiples the downside is 13% to 21%, cushioned by a 6.2% to 6.6% dividend yield. At the five-year low multiple (9.09x) the shares would be worth EUR 16.2 (-13%); at the ten-year 10th percentile (8.7x), EUR 15.5 (-17%); and at 8.7x with a 5% EPS cut as well, EUR 14.8 (-21%). The brokers' bear cases are Morgan Stanley at EUR 15.20 and Axia at EUR 14.40. The tail that a single-country company cannot diversify is a sovereign crisis: in 2012 OTE traded at six times earnings and three times EBITDA, and Deutsche Bank's devaluation case is EUR 5.70. That tail is now remote, with an A- sovereign rating, primary budget surpluses and government debt falling to about 129% of output by 2027.

OTE has little cyclicality, and the sector precedents that fit point to slow wholesale pressure rather than a sudden shock. Connectivity is non-discretionary, and OTE absorbed the 2022 to 2023 energy shock with flat EBITDA; the only cycle with amplitude is public ICT, which carries little profit. Two precedents fit. The first is utility-backed fibre: Open Fiber against Telecom Italia brought a decade of wholesale pressure that ended in consolidation, and in Ireland eir kept 66% of fibre broadband against SIRO's 27%. The second is "slow growth punished twice": low-single-digit growers de-rate on multiple and earnings together.

Where I differ from the market. Where the market prices risk at all, it prices retail competition: Morgan Stanley's bear case is "intensified competition" at 4.5x EV/EBITDA. I price wholesale erosion and a political filter on pricing, both of which are slower and more trackable. I also weight sentiment risk more heavily than the published research, which treats the multiple as an output of the fundamentals.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that concentrating the case in one politically exposed decision makes the 18-month path more binary than a 1.4% growth rate implies. I would judge the case riskier if the first-quarter 2027 print showed churn rising with the price step, if a Greek authority challenged the indexation clause, or if Nova's buyer were a strategic owner with a stated partnership with the Vodafone-PPC venture.
Conclusion: fundamentally, OTE is one of the simplest and lowest-risk cases in European telecoms, with a narrow, early-resolving earnings range and a wide, Greek-driven price range; the risk to the shares is the multiple, not the model.
Score: 75, set by the Rater. The fundamental case is simple and narrow: one country and currency, fixed-rate debt, mechanical below EBITDA, a formulaic payout, and a FY2027 EPS cone of EUR 1.62-1.75 around 1.69 (about -4% to +3.5%) with 70-75% probability within 2-4%, resolving within twelve weeks; low cyclicality (the 2022-23 energy shock absorbed with flat EBITDA). It is held off the top by a political binary on the price step (15-25%), a longer FY2028 left tail from the wholesale venture and Nova's buyer, and a Greek, flow-driven multiple (MSCI transition, a 36.6% free float) that makes the price cone about four times the EPS cone; coherent with the Risks groups (70, 74).

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Judgement: the dashboard's rule places OTE at "Turning/Inflecting"; I think the turn has already happened, and OTE is now in a phase where its cash return is reinforcing while its growth narrative stalls, with the next phase set by one event in February 2027.

The turn is behind OTE. The two-year-forward P/E re-rated from about 9x (2023 to early 2025) to about 11x (mid-2026), as the PPC fear cleared at retail, Romania was sold, the payout was codified, the first explicit guide was set above consensus, S&P upgraded OTE and Greece was reclassified. The share price rose from EUR 13.7 (March 2025) to EUR 20 (July 2026). The internal change programme is delivered.

The evidence argues against "broadening". OTE has no new lever and no numbered ambition; core service growth has decelerated from 5.5% to 2.0%; retail fixed revenue is falling; the share of Buy ratings is down 15 points, with Sell and Hold ratings appearing; and the share price is 4.5% lower over three months.

The evidence favours "reinforcing" rather than "stalling". The cash loop is intact and growing (the dividend grows 7% to 8% a year, and the buyback retires 2.5% of the shares a year). The February 2027 dividend will beat consensus. Index inclusion and cheaper spectrum are dated positives. And the price step, if applied, restarts core growth.

February 2027 is the fork, and both branches will be visible within about twelve weeks, which is unusual: most stalls are diagnosed late. A full price step and an "about +3%" guide would read as reinforcing: the indexation habit confirmed, the yield growing and Greece re-rating. No price step and a "+1% to +2%" guide would read as stalling: a 1% grower on a Greek yield multiple, with a wholesale erosion story forming. The phase after that depends more on Greece (the election and MSCI) than on OTE.

Where I differ from the market. Three readings compete. The dashboard rule says OTE is turning up; the lead broker's "a new OTE" framing says the thesis is broadening; the new Sell and Hold ratings say it is stalling. I think the honest reading is that OTE has completed its turn and is now a mature cash compounder whose narrative has stalled while its cash generation has not. The reading matters for the fair multiple (#11): a turning-up stock earns a multiple above its median, because its forecasts are about to improve; a reinforcing cash stock earns about its median; and a stalling stock earns below its median.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The case for "turning up" is that the price step becomes an annual habit, consensus starts to model it, and the market re-rates OTE from a Greek yield stock to a European "contractual pricing" incumbent at Orange Polska's multiples. That outcome requires a February with both a full price step and an upward guide, followed by a first quarter that shows the step in the mobile line; I put the combination at about 20% to 25%.
Conclusion: OTE's turn is complete, its cash loop is reinforcing and its growth narrative is stalling; February 2027 decides which word the market uses.
Score: 48, set by the Rater. I agree with the memo rather than the computed Turning/Inflecting: the turn (9x to 11x, PPC fear cleared, Romania sold, payout codified, Greece reclassified) is behind it, and the stock is a cash-reinforcing compounder with a stalling growth narrative (core service growth 5.5% to 2.0%, retail fixed negative, buy share -15 points, price -4.5% over three months), with a February fork between reinforcing and stalling. The good news is largely known and no broadening lever exists, so it sits a little below Solid State's plausible turn and just above CVS Group's credible bottoming with slightly negative revisions.

#11 The fair multiple

Judgement: the guideline fair multiple is 12.5x (the 60th percentile of OTE's ten-year two-year-forward P/E, 13% above the 11.05x the dashboard shows today); my view is that 11.8x, the ten-year median, is the defensible central figure, and that 12.5x is right only if the price step is applied in full and the Greek re-rating continues through the election and the MSCI transition.

OTE's ten-year range runs from 8.7x to 15.9x, and neither of its past regimes fits today exactly. The ten-year percentiles are 8.7x at the 10th ("crash"), 10.8x at the 35th ("conservative"), 11.8x at the median ("prudent"), 13.8x at the 75th ("defendable") and 15.9x at the 90th ("mania"). The five-year range is 9.1x to 14.0x, with a median of 10.3x; today's multiple sits at the 58th percentile of that range. The 13x to 18x years (2016 to 2019) coincided with double-digit EPS growth from falling depreciation and with a Greek risk premium falling from crisis levels. The 9x to 10x years (2023 to early 2025) coincided with the PPC fear, the Romanian cash drain and no payout policy. OTE today has no growth engine, which argues for the five-year frame; but Greece is now an A- developed market and OTE's cash policy is codified, which argues against a return to the 2023 to 2025 lows.

Five reasons make 11.8x, not 12.5x, my central fair multiple.

  1. Lifecycle phase: a reinforcing cash stock with a stalled growth narrative earns about its median multiple, not the 60th percentile reserved for a stock whose forecasts are turning up (#10).
  2. Reinvestment: OTE has little high-return reinvestment (fibre earns low single-digit returns until utilisation passes 50% to 60%, and ICT is low-margin), so OTE's value is cash yield plus multiple. That profile deserves a yield-stock multiple near the sector median two-year-forward P/E of about 11.8x, not a compounder's multiple.
  3. No catch-up: the market is not going to catch up with my assessment (#7), so a re-rating has to come from Greece or from the price step, and neither is in the base case.
  4. Peers: peers of similar quality and parental control trade far lower (Telekom Austria 8.1x, Proximus 7.8x, Deutsche Telekom 9.4x, Magyar Telekom 9.4x); only Orange Polska (16x) trades higher, on a real change force.
  5. Yield cross-check: at 11.8x today's two-year-forward EPS, the FY2026 dividend yields 5.0%; at 12.5x, 4.7%. Against a Greek ten-year bond yield of 3.3%, a spread of 140 to 170 basis points for a dividend growing 7% a year is fair, not generous.

12.5x is nevertheless reachable, because OTE's multiple is driven by the company and by Greece, not by the sector. About 90% of OTE's multiple is company- and country-driven (the sector explains only 2% of the variance), and OTE re-rated 20% in 2025 to 2026 against a falling sector. Four events would each add 0.3x to 0.5x: a clean election (the ruling party is 10 points ahead), MSCI inclusion absorbed without emerging-market selling dominating, a full price step, and a Vodafone-PPC venture closing with slow migration. Together they would take the stock through 12.5x towards the 75th percentile (13.8x). Even at 12.5x, OTE's dividend yield spread over Greek bonds (about 140 basis points) is wider than many European yield stocks offer.

Where I differ from the market. The mean broker target (EUR 20.88) implies about 11.5x to 12x two-year-forward EPS, close to my figure. Morgan Stanley's EUR 23.80 implies about 13x on its own numbers, and Barclays' EUR 18.00 about 10x. I sit with the median broker on the multiple, and below the lead broker.
Counter-case and what would change my view. If February brings the full price step and an "about +3%" guide, and the first-quarter mobile line confirms them, I would move my central figure to 12.5x, because OTE's phase would then genuinely be turning up on earnings and not only on cash. If the price step is blocked or Nova's buyer joins the Vodafone-PPC venture, 10.8x (the 35th percentile) becomes the right anchor.
Conclusion: 11.8x is my fair multiple; 12.5x is a reasonable upside case that requires Greece and the price step to cooperate; and the gap between the two multiples is worth about 7 points of 18-month return.
Score: 79, set by the Rater. Cheap on one measure and neutral on the other gives B. Part of the cheapness against peers is deserved, because the ten-year average premium (1.15x) was earned in the D&A-collapse years of double-digit EPS growth and OTE now grows more slowly than its cohort with a stalling narrative that earns about its median (the memo's fair 11.8x against 10.8x today), so I place it in the lower half of the band rather than at the floor, as the own-range reading also leans cheap.

#12 Total shareholder return, by component

Judgement: at the guideline multiple the model's return is +36% over 18 months (to 31 March 2028) and +50% over three years (to 30 September 2029); about half of the 18-month return and two-thirds of the three-year return comes from high-probability cash and earnings mechanics, and the rest comes from the multiple.

The model splits the guideline return into dividends, earnings growth and re-rating, on a two-year-forward basis.

HorizonTotal returnAnnualisedFrom dividendsFrom the multiple (10.8x to 12.5x)From earnings (two-year-forward EPS)
18-month column, 31 March 2028+36.3%+24.8%+11.1%+16.1%+7.8%
Three-year column, 30 September 2029+50.0%+15.0%+17.0%+16.1%+14.6%

Each leg of the return has a different source and a different certainty.

  • Dividends (+11.1%, EUR 2.08 a share): the dividends declared for FY2026 (EUR 1.02, paid July 2027) and FY2027 (EUR 1.07, paid July 2028), both set by the payout formula on cash that is already largely visible. The buyback's contribution sits in the earnings leg, not here.
  • Earnings (+7.8%): two-year-forward EPS rolls from about EUR 1.74 today (a blend of FY2027 and FY2028) to about EUR 1.88 (a blend of FY2029 and FY2030). Roughly 60% of that growth is the share count falling 2.5% a year and 40% is net income growing 1.7% a year; both are mechanical.
  • Multiple (+16.1%): the move from 10.8x to 12.5x, which is the judgement in #11.

The earnings and multiple legs multiply, and the dividend leg adds.

My view of the return depends on the exit multiple, and each multiple needs a specific set of events.

The dividend and earnings legs are the investment case: they set a floor under the return that most European telecoms cannot offer. Those two legs deliver 19% over 18 months and 32% over three years with 70% to 75% confidence, from a business that lands its guidance and distributes its cash. Even at the ten-year 10th-percentile multiple, the 18-month return is about zero and the three-year return is positive.

The multiple leg is the variance, and its drivers are dated and Greek. They are the price step (December to February), the guide and distribution (25 February), the MSCI pricing window (late April), the election (May to July) and the clearance of the Vodafone-PPC venture (first half of 2027). The return is therefore not a bet on OTE beating anything; it is a bet that OTE keeps doing what it does while Greece keeps the multiple at or above its median.

The upside tails are capital decisions, and the downside tail is the wholesale venture plus a political block on pricing. A pass-through of the tax windfall adds about 2% to EPS (as buyback) or 2% of the share price in cash (as dividend); releveraging adds 23% to EPS. The downside tail costs 5% to 10% of EPS over two years and probably a turn of multiple.

Where I differ from the market. The mean target implies about +11% plus the dividend yield, roughly my 11.8x case with a lower earnings leg; the lead broker's EUR 23.80 is close to the guideline case. The market does not frame the return as cash plus multiple with a floor. It frames the return as value, a 22% to 28% EV/EBITDA discount to the sector that should close. I think that discount is structural (governance, growth and liquidity) and will close only to the extent that Greece re-rates.
Counter-case and what would change my view. The counter-case is that the "floor" assumes OTE honours the payout formula through the spectrum year, and that the roll-forward of two-year-forward EPS is not interrupted by the fast wholesale tail. A mechanical 2028 distribution on FY2027 free cash flow of EUR 516m would cut the dividend leg by about EUR 0.15 a share. I would raise my central return to the guideline case on a full price step in February; I would lower it to the unchanged-multiple case if the step is capped or the Vodafone-PPC venture closes with a stated migration plan.
Conclusion: the return is about 19% of near-certain cash and per-share mechanics over 18 months, plus or minus the multiple Greece pays, which makes it a high-floor, moderate-ceiling return rather than an upgrade-driven one.
Score: 81, set by the Rater. About 27% sits in the B band (20-35%) at about 82 on the scale; I hold it at 81 because about 9 points of the central return depend on re-rating towards the median, while the skew is unusually benign (about 19% from dividends and per-share mechanics at an unchanged multiple, about nil at the ten-year 10th-percentile multiple), so I do not move it down further, and the three-year +43% supports it.

#13 Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

OTE is a superb franchise in a bounded field. OTE takes 93% of its industry's operating free cash flow, earns a 42% margin that rises to 45% on mix and a 29% return on equity, carries 0.5x leverage, enjoys state-granted protections, and has seen a half-price entrant fail. OTE is run by an honest tracker that has never missed a number it set and never raised one, within a parent's frame that forbids growth risk and balance-sheet action and mandates cash upstreaming.

The change programme that re-rated the stock from 9x to 11x is finished; what remains is a cash machine and two decisions by outside actors. The cash machine is an 8% yield growing 7% a year. The first outside decision is Greek politics on the annual price step, which is the whole of FY2027's growth. The second is the speed at which Vodafone (and Nova) migrate wholesale lines, which is the whole of the FY2028 to FY2030 risk. The earnings range is narrow and resolves early; the price range is wide and Greek.

The most attractive feature of the return is its floor. The model's +36% at 12.5x is a fair description of the upside case, and my central case is about +29% at 11.8x. Because half the return is cash and per-share mechanics and half is the multiple, the return is near zero even at a crash multiple.

OTE is not a stock on which guidance, estimates or the narrative will move materially higher. OTE is a stock to own for the cash and the Greek re-rating, while watching one tariff schedule in December 2026 and one results day on 25 February 2027.
